title: Do Black Hole Spins Hint at a New Particle?
hook: Heavy merging black holes spin slower than light ones. One explanation: a featherweight boson grows a cloud around fast spinners and drains their rotation away.
key_points: Superradiance lets a spinning black hole hand rotational energy to an ultralight boson, growing a bound cloud around itself.
The effect is resonant: a given boson mass only drains black holes in a matching mass range, imprinting a mass-spin relation.
The authors build a superradiance-informed spin distribution model and fit it to the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA merger catalogs.
A scalar boson of mass around 10^-12 eV reproduces the observed mass-spin correlation.
Support strengthens as the catalog grows, reaching a Bayes factor of about ln B = 7.8 for GWTC-5.0.
That mass range overlaps a earlier independent estimate from waveform analysis of the single event GW190728.
content_html: Now that gravitational-wave catalogs hold hundreds of black hole mergers, astronomers can ask population questions rather than event-by-event ones. One pattern that has emerged is a relationship between a black hole's mass and its spin. A new analysis argues that the pattern is what you'd expect if a very light, so-far-undiscovered boson exists.
extra_html: The mechanism is black hole superradiance: a spinning black hole amplifies waves of a sufficiently light bosonic field, and if those waves stay gravitationally bound they grow into an oscillating cloud, paid for out of the hole's rotational energy. Crucially the process is resonant — it only runs efficiently when the boson's Compton wavelength is comparable to the black hole's size — so a single boson mass spins down black holes in one mass band and leaves others alone. Xiao-Xiao Kou, Vuk Mandic, Ran Ding, and Chi Tian encode this in an extended spin distribution model and compare it against the Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalogs. They report that a scalar of mass around 10^-12 eV matches the observed mass-spin relation, with support growing as the catalog does: the Bayes factor reaches about ln B = 7.8 for GWTC-5.0. They also note the mass range coincides with a previous, independent estimate drawn from the waveform of GW190728. It is a population-level hint rather than a detection, and astrophysical formation channels can also shape spins — but it is the kind of claim more data will sharpen quickly.

related.title: Hunting Hypothetical Particles in the Hair of Black Holes
related.hook: If ultralight bosons exist, a spinning black hole would grow a cloud of them and hum for years. LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA listened to two merger remnants, heard nothing, and ruled out a band of masses.

related.title: Ten Years of Listening to Black Holes Spin
related.hook: A decade after the first gravitational-wave detection, 100+ events let astronomers read black holes' spins — and spin turns out to reveal how the pairs were born.

related.title: 390 Gravitational Waves In, and Black Hole Astronomy Is Just Getting Started
related.hook: The latest gravitational-wave catalog leaps to 390 confirmed detections — including the clearest signal ever caught and evidence some black holes are built from earlier mergers.

related.title: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
related.hook: Everything we can see — stars, planets, people — is only about 5% of the universe. The other 95% is two mysteries we've never directly detected.

flashcards.prompt: How does superradiance let a black hole lose spin to a hypothetical particle?
flashcards.back_html: A spinning black hole amplifies waves of an ultralight boson, which stay gravitationally bound and grow into a cloud. The energy comes out of the hole's rotation, so it spins down.

flashcards.prompt: Why would superradiance produce a relationship between black hole mass and spin?

choices.text: The effect is resonant, so a given boson mass only spins down holes in a matching mass range
Heavier black holes always form from slower-spinning stars
Superradiance adds spin to heavy holes and removes it from light ones

flashcards.explanation_html: Superradiant growth requires the boson's Compton wavelength to roughly match the hole's size, so only a band of black hole masses is affected — leaving a signature in the mass-spin plane.

flashcards.prompt: What boson mass do the authors find fits the gravitational-wave catalogs?
flashcards.back_html: About 10^-12 eV — a scalar so light it is some 20 orders of magnitude below the electron mass.
